questions.q: A URL shortener must count every click and be able to disable a bad link immediately. Which redirect?
questions.why: Browsers cache a 301, so repeat clicks never reach you: analytics are lost and a disabled link keeps working for them. A 302 brings every click back to your service.

questions.q: What does a browser do differently after a 301 compared with a 302?
choices: It remembers the redirect and goes straight to the long URL next time
It shows the user a warning
questions.why: Both send the long URL in the Location header. Only the 301 is remembered, so later clicks skip your service.

questions.q: Click counts use write-behind: Redis counts, and a job adds each link's delta to the DB every ~30 s. What do you lose if Redis crashes?
choices: Up to one flush interval of clicks
questions.why: Counts not yet flushed are lost (up to ~30 s). Fine for analytics; mappings, which you can't lose, are written durably.

questions.q: Why not write every click through to a SQL row at 50k clicks/s on one link?
choices: SQL can't store integers that big
All writes hit ONE row and wait on its lock; a primary does ~5k writes/s in total
questions.why: Write-through sends 50k/s to one hot row. Write-behind turns that into one DB write per flush.

questions.q: Why not track per-link click counts in Prometheus (metrics)?
choices: One series per short code is billions of series; metrics stores fall over on that cardinality
Metrics are too slow to write
questions.why: Metrics systems are for low-cardinality totals like redirects/s. Per-entity counters belong in a store like Redis.

questions.q: A celebrity link gets 30k clicks/s against a service sized for 16k/s. Best fix?
choices: Put a queue in front of the redirect service
Give the link its own replica behind the service
Cache the 302 at a CDN with a short max-age
questions.why: Everyone clicking that link gets the same answer, so the CDN serves it from the edge; the service sees about one request per edge location per max-age.
questions.note: Spikes on a hot link: CDN, not a queue

questions.q: Why doesn't a queue help with redirect spikes?
choices: The browser is waiting for the 302, so queued requests just time out later
questions.why: Queues help work nobody waits on (click events, bulk imports). A synchronous request still needs an answer within the client's timeout.
questions.note: Spikes on a hot link: CDN, not a queue

questions.q: The CDN caches each 302 for 60 s. What do you give up?
choices: A deleted or expired link keeps working for up to 60 s
questions.why: Fix with a short max-age or a CDN purge on delete. You also stop seeing every click; count them from CDN access logs.
questions.note: Spikes on a hot link: CDN, not a queue
